lines.text: A tiny town in Ohio just fired its mayor because he greenlit a data centre for Meta.
Data centres are big buildings full of computers that mainly just run AI nowadays, so it's sacked over a building.
So what just happened to AI with the midterms in America and where does AI get built when the residents of towns say no?
Let's find out.
Meta wanted a giant data centre for more AI and the mayor said yes.
A data centre uses as much electricity as a small city.
Picture living in Piqua, this little town, and opening your power bill to find you're chipping in for the new power lines, right?
So then the residents of Piqua voted.
Should we ban the big data centres?
Yes.
And that was two to one.
Should we sack the mayor?
That was even more, 70% of the residents.
The landslide.
But Meta's data centre was already being built.
So Piqua now has a data centre going up in the town that just banned them.
Meta says it will work with local officials which is kind of their party line every time they do something which everyone hates, which is a lot.
So when small towns say no, the AI companies have to find that power somewhere else.
and they have to pay for it.
And I reckon that cost lands in your electricity subscription and your business's AI subscriptions.

So now when we renew an AI tool we might see special deals to change over to new plans when secretly they charge you more than you'd pay if you'd stuck to your current terms on the premise of bonus credits and things like that.
I've seen this happen three times in the last week with businesses with AI tools.
And it will continue because if it's a little town like Piqua, the fight ends up on my bill in one way or another.
The full story is at makeyourmindup.ai.
